$comment: Prisma CLI commands that can reach production. Merged into the core guard when this stack is active. Every pattern has a test case in .claude/hooks/tests/guard-cases.json.
$targetProblem: Prisma differs from the Supabase CLI in the way that matters here: it has no --local flag and no linked-project state. Every command takes its target from DATABASE_URL, read from the environment or a .env file. So the command text alone NEVER says which database is about to be changed, and `npx prisma migrate reset` is identical whether it wipes a scratch database or production. The rules below therefore require the target to be stated in the command, which is the only place the guard can see it.

deny.$comment: The one that matches the scenario this whole guard exists for: it drops the database and recreates it from migrations. There is no confirmation prompt with --force, and none at all in a non-interactive shell — which is what an unattended run is.
deny.reason: prisma migrate reset DROPS the database and recreates it. Which database is decided by DATABASE_URL, which is not visible in this command. Put the target in the command so it can be read: DATABASE_URL=postgresql://…@localhost:5432/dev npx prisma migrate reset

deny.$comment: --accept-data-loss is Prisma asking a question and being told not to ask. Dropping columns and tables is exactly what it accepts.
deny.reason: prisma db push --accept-data-loss drops whatever columns and tables the schema no longer describes. The flag exists to suppress the warning that would otherwise stop this.

prisma db push writes the schema straight to a database with no migration file, so nothing records what changed. Its target is DATABASE_URL, which this command does not state. Put the target in the command.

deny.$comment: Arbitrary SQL, usually from a file the guard cannot read. Every sql-* rule in the base set is bypassed by putting the statement in that file.
deny.reason: prisma db execute runs arbitrary SQL, normally from a file this guard cannot inspect. Whatever the file contains is invisible here.

deny.$comment: Not destructive itself, which is why it is easy to wave through. It edits the migration history to say a migration was applied when it was not, so the NEXT deploy runs against a schema nobody has verified.
deny.reason: prisma migrate resolve rewrites migration history to mark a migration applied or rolled back without running it. The database and the history then disagree, and the next deploy is the one that fails.

prisma migrate deploy applies pending migrations to whatever DATABASE_URL points at, which this command does not state. Migrations reach production through the deployment pipeline, not from a developer machine. State the target if this is local.

prisma-studio: prisma studio opens a browser client onto DATABASE_URL, with full read AND write access, and is
not blocked. It is interactive: a human is at the keyboard by definition, which is the condition
every rule here is trying to restore. Blocking it would cost a tool used constantly in local
development and buy nothing an agent could not do more directly.
prisma-migrate-dev: prisma migrate dev is not blocked, though it CAN drop and recreate on drift. It refuses to run
against a non-development database by design, and blocking it would stop the ordinary act of
authoring a migration -- which is most of what Prisma work is. The line is drawn at commands that
will act on any target they are given.

$unlessNote: `unless` is matched against the command as typed. It cannot be folded into the pattern as a negative lookahead: the guard also matches a variant with leading environment assignments stripped, so the DATABASE_URL being offered as evidence is gone from that variant and the rule fires anyway. Stating the target is the only way a Prisma command says which database it will act on, so the exception has to be able to see it.
